title: `var` infers a local's type from its initializer
scope:
a second spelling for a local variable declaration, alongside `rule:types/declaration`'s typed one.
Nothing else — parameters, properties, constants, `foreach`/destructuring bindings, closures and
returns all still require a written type.

summary.headline: `var $n = expr;` declares a local with the type of its initializer
summary.body:
`var $count = 0;` gives `$count` the type `int`, fixed for its whole life exactly as if `int`
had been written. The type is whatever the initializer already has — honest, not clever: `var
$id = Core\Request::query('id');` is `mixed`, because that is what the call returns. An
initializer is required. A bare array literal is the one refused shape: `var $x = [1, 2];` stops
the build and names `array<T> $x = [1, 2];` as the fix, because an array literal takes its type
from where it lands rather than supplying one.
